questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has had 4 days of burning, tingling pain over the left side of her lower back and flank. Yesterday a band of clustered vesicles on a red base appeared in the same area, stopping sharply at the midline. Her temperature is 37.9°C. She had chickenpox as a child.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Burning pain then unilateral dermatomal vesicles in an older adult who had chickenpox is shingles.

steps.x: Pain before the rash, a unilateral band, previous chickenpox.

elim: Itchy rash at a contact site, not dermatomal pain before vesicles.
Itchy symmetrical vesicles on elbows and buttocks with coeliac disease.
Recurs at the lips or genitals, not a painful dermatomal band.
Loin pain without any rash.

steps.x: D: Herpes zoster. Painful, dermatomal, vesicular, unilateral = shingles (reactivation of VZV).

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl at nursery has had a mild fever and been off her food for a day. She now has an itchy rash that began on her scalp and spread to her face and trunk. Examination shows red macules, papules, clear vesicles and some crusted lesions all at the same time.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A prodrome then a scalp-to-trunk itchy rash with lesions at all stages together is chickenpox.

steps.x: Fever, scalp onset, lesions at different stages together.

elim: Vesicles on the palms, soles and mouth.
Golden crusted lesions, usually around the mouth, without a prodrome.
A maculopapular rash starting behind the ears with Koplik spots.
Itchy burrows in finger webs, no fever or vesicles at all stages.

steps.x: A: Chickenpox. Macules, papules, vesicles and crusts at once = chickenpox (primary VZV).

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a 3 day history of a painful vesicular rash over the right forehead and scalp. On examination there are also vesicles on the tip of his nose. His visual acuity is currently normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely significance of the lesions on the nose?
o: Nasociliary nerve involvement with a high risk of eye complications
questions.e: Hutchinson's sign (vesicles on the nasal tip) shows nasociliary involvement and a threefold risk of ocular complications.

clues: vesicles on the tip of his nose
steps.x: Ophthalmic division rash plus nasal tip vesicles.

elim: Would cause honey crusting or pus, not a sign of nerve involvement.
Ramsay Hunt affects the ear and facial nerve.
The nasal tip is supplied by the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic nerve.
The nose tip is midline from the same ophthalmic division.

steps.x: D: Nasociliary nerve involvement with a high risk of eye complications. Hutchinson's sign = nasociliary nerve = threefold risk of ophthalmic zoster.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman had shingles in the right T4 dermatome 5 months ago. The rash has completely healed, leaving faint scars, but she still has burning, stabbing pain and the touch of her clothing on the area is unbearable.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Persistent neuropathic pain in a dermatome after the shingles rash has healed is post-herpetic neuralgia.

clues: touch of her clothing on the area is unbearable
steps.x: Pain persists months after the rash resolved.

elim: Exertional chest pain, not burning pain with allodynia in a healed dermatome.
Tender costal cartilages, not a dermatomal burning pain.
Would have new vesicles.
Requires trauma and causes point tenderness.

steps.x: C: Post-herpetic neuralgia. Pain persisting after the rash resolves = post-herpetic neuralgia.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has shingles affecting the left ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Five days after the rash appeared he develops a painful red left eye, photophobia and blurred vision.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with eye involvement
questions.e: Ophthalmic division shingles can cause keratitis and uveitis, presenting with a painful red eye and blurred vision.

steps.x: A shingles rash in V1 followed by a painful red eye.

elim: Causes a fixed mid-dilated pupil and halos, unrelated to shingles.
Sticky discharge without photophobia or loss of vision.
Gritty eyelid margins, no photophobia or blurring.
A painless red patch with normal vision.

steps.x: D: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with eye involvement. Ophthalmic zoster is a key complication; urgent ophthalmology review.

questions.stem: A 5 year old boy has had chickenpox for 6 days. Several lesions on his legs have become larger, red, hot and painful with yellow pus. He is otherwise well with a temperature of 37.8°C and pulse rate 104 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Red, hot, purulent lesions in a well child with chickenpox are a secondary bacterial skin infection.

steps.x: Localised infected spots in a well child.

elim: Affects a fetus exposed in the first trimester.
Causes confusion, ataxia or seizures.
Would cause severe disproportionate pain and systemic illness.
A complication of shingles in older adults.

steps.x: E: Secondary bacterial infection. Secondary bacterial infection is a common complication of VZV skin lesions.

questions.stem: A newborn girl is small for gestational age. Her right arm is short and underdeveloped and she has scarred, zig-zag skin lesions on the same side. Her mother, who had no immunity to chickenpox, had a vesicular rash at 11 weeks of pregnancy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: First-trimester maternal chickenpox in a non-immune mother causes low birth weight, limb hypoplasia and skin scarring.

steps.x: Non-immune mother, first-trimester rash, limb hypoplasia and scarring.

elim: Causes limb constriction rings, unrelated to maternal infection.
Causes microcephaly, deafness and hepatosplenomegaly.
Causes cataracts, deafness and heart defects.
Infection near delivery causing vesicles and encephalitis.

steps.x: D: Congenital varicella syndrome. First-trimester chickenpox in a non-immune mother = risk of congenital varicella syndrome.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with rheumatoid arthritis takes methotrexate and has recently started a TNF-alpha inhibitor. He develops a painful unilateral band of vesicles across his right chest wall. He asks why he has got this at his age.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason he developed this condition?
o: A new exposure to herpes simplex
First exposure to varicella zoster virus
Low antibody levels from vitamin D deficiency
questions.e: Shingles reactivates when cell-mediated immunity falls, as with immunosuppressive drugs.

steps.x: Immunosuppression and a dermatomal rash.

elim: Herpes simplex does not cause dermatomal vesicles.
Drug rashes are generalised, not a painful dermatomal band.
First exposure causes chickenpox, not dermatomal shingles.
Not a mechanism of shingles reactivation.

steps.x: E: Reduced cell-mediated immunity. Shingles affects older adults and the immunosuppressed: falling cell-mediated immunity.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has 3 days of severe burning pain in a strip running from his left lower back round to the left groin. There is no rash yet. His temperature is 37.8°C. Urine dipstick and abdominal examination are normal. Two days later vesicles appear along the same strip.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Burning dermatomal pain and fever often precede the vesicular rash of shingles.

clues: vesicles appear along the same strip
steps.x: Pain in a band, then vesicles in the same band.

elim: Back pain with a pulsatile mass and no vesicles.
A groin lump, no rash or dermatomal pain.
Pain radiates down the leg, without vesicles.
Fever and loin pain with an abnormal dipstick.

steps.x: E: Shingles. Pain and fever often come before the rash of shingles.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has had chickenpox for 7 days. His mother notes that the spots are no longer itchy and every lesion has now dried and crusted. He is well, eating normally and afebrile.
questions.q: Which is the most likely next course of his illness?
o: Resolution over the next few days
Spread of new vesicles to the palms
questions.e: Chickenpox resolves over about a week; once all lesions are crusted the illness is ending.

clues: every lesion has now dried and crusted
steps.x: Day 7, all lesions crusted, well child.

elim: A complication of shingles in older adults.
There are no signs of severe pain or systemic illness.
Primary infection gives lasting immunity.
New crops stop once lesions crust.

steps.x: D: Resolution over the next few days. Chickenpox resolves over about one week.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant develops chickenpox. She has never had chickenpox and has not been vaccinated. She asks about the risk to her baby.
questions.q: Which is the most likely risk to the fetus?
questions.e: Non-immune first-trimester chickenpox risks congenital varicella syndrome.

steps.x: Non-immune, first trimester.

elim: Linked to maternal anti-Ro antibodies.
Linked to parvovirus B19.
Linked to genital herpes around delivery.
Linked to folate deficiency and antiepileptics.

steps.x: B: Congenital varicella syndrome. First-trimester chickenpox = congenital varicella syndrome risk.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man had shingles in the left T8 dermatome 3 weeks ago and the vesicles have crusted. He still has severe burning and shooting pain there that keeps him awake. Paracetamol and ibuprofen have not helped. He has no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Severe neuropathic pain after shingles is treated with gabapentin, low-dose pregabalin, amitriptyline or duloxetine.

clues: Paracetamol and ibuprofen have not helped
steps.x: Neuropathic pain not controlled by simple analgesia.

elim: Opioids are not first-line for neuropathic pain.
The rash has healed; antivirals do not treat the pain.
Not used for neuropathic pain after shingles.
Does not treat neuropathic pain.

steps.x: B: Gabapentin. Neuropathic pain/post-herpetic neuralgia: gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline or duloxetine.

questions.stem: A 30 year old nurse asks why her grandfather has shingles, when she thought that was the same virus as the chickenpox she caught from him as a child.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate explanation?
o: Shingles is a new primary infection caught from a child
Shingles is an allergic reaction to the chickenpox vaccine
Shingles is caused by a bacterium in the nerve
Shingles is caused by herpes simplex type 1
Shingles is reactivation of varicella zoster virus that caused earlier chickenpox
questions.e: Chickenpox is primary VZV infection; shingles is reactivation of latent virus.

steps.x: One virus, two diseases.

elim: Primary infection causes chickenpox.
Not an allergy.
VZV is a virus.
Herpes simplex causes cold sores, not shingles.

steps.x: E: Shingles is reactivation of varicella zoster virus that caused earlier chickenpox. Varicella = primary infection; herpes zoster = reactivation of latent virus.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl has a 2 day history of fever followed by an itchy rash spreading from her scalp to her trunk, with macules, papules, vesicles and crusts. Several classmates have chickenpox. She is well and drinking normally.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Chickenpox and shingles are usually diagnosed clinically; PCR is only used if uncertain.

steps.x: A classic rash with a contact history.

elim: Does not confirm the diagnosis.
Invasive and unnecessary.
Used for streptococcal infection.
Only needed if the diagnosis is uncertain.

steps.x: B: No test; diagnose clinically. Clinical diagnosis; VZV PCR only if uncertain.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman on chemotherapy for lymphoma has a 2 day history of scattered painful vesicles on her trunk, some in a band and some outside it. Her GP is unsure whether this is VZV or herpes simplex.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: If the diagnosis is uncertain, VZV PCR from vesicle fluid confirms it.

steps.x: An atypical rash in an immunosuppressed patient with diagnostic doubt.

elim: Do not detect viruses in skin lesions.
Used for contact allergy.
Used for fungal infection and scabies.
Shows past immunity, not current infection.

steps.x: E: VZV PCR of vesicle fluid. If uncertain: PCR of vesicle fluid; IgG only shows immunity.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant tells her midwife that her son's friend, whom she played with yesterday, now has chickenpox. She cannot remember whether she ever had chickenpox. She has no rash.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox with uncertain immunity should have VZV IgG checked.

clues: cannot remember whether she ever had chickenpox
steps.x: Exposure in pregnancy with unknown immunity.

elim: Only assesses the fetus later.
Does not show immunity.
Shows recent infection, not past immunity.
She has no lesions; PCR does not assess immunity.

steps.x: C: Varicella zoster IgG. Uncertain immunity in pregnancy: check varicella zoster IgG.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 28 weeks pregnant was exposed to a cousin with chickenpox 2 days ago. She is not sure of her immunity and has no rash. She is well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Check varicella zoster IgG and await the result
questions.e: After 20 weeks with no rash, check IgG and await results before acting.

steps.x: Over 20 weeks, exposed, no rash.

elim: There is no indication.
Her immunity is unknown.
She has no rash and is well.
With no rash after 20 weeks, check IgG and await results first.

steps.x: B: Check varicella zoster IgG and await the result. Over 20 weeks and no rash: check IgG and wait.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has a 3 day history of a painful band of vesicles over the right T6 dermatome which do not cross the midline. Before the rash she had 2 days of burning pain in the same area. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to diagnosis?
o: Clinical diagnosis from the history and rash
questions.e: Shingles is diagnosed clinically from painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles.

steps.x: A classic dermatomal picture.

elim: Not needed for shingles.
Not needed; no neurological deficit.
An old test that is not used.
Most adults are IgG positive; it does not show reactivation.

steps.x: A: Clinical diagnosis from the history and rash. Shingles is usually a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant is a primary school teacher. A child in her class developed chickenpox yesterday. She grew up abroad and has no record of chickenpox or vaccination. She has no rash.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Test immunity with VZV IgG in an exposed pregnant woman of unknown status.

clues: no record of chickenpox or vaccination
steps.x: First-trimester exposure with unknown immunity.

elim: Invasive and not a test of maternal immunity.
Only for suspected varicella pneumonia.
Not a test of immunity.
Detects active infection, not immunity.

steps.x: D: Varicella zoster IgG. Non-immune risk in pregnancy: test VZV IgG.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 1 day history of a painful vesicular rash over the left L1 dermatome. He is otherwise well, with normal renal function and no immunosuppression. He has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral aciclovir 200 mg twice daily for 3 days
Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
questions.e: Shingles is treated with aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days.

steps.x: Early shingles in a well adult.

elim: Too low a dose and too short.
An antibacterial, not antiviral.
Not a treatment for shingles.
Used for cold sores, not shingles.

steps.x: B: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days. Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with shingles over the right T12 dermatome is prescribed oral aciclovir. She finds taking tablets five times a day difficult and asks whether there is an alternative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate alternative?
questions.e: Valaciclovir and famciclovir are alternatives to aciclovir, taken less often.

steps.x: She needs a less frequent antiviral.

elim: An antibacterial.
An antifungal.
Treats influenza.
An antiretroviral for HIV.

steps.x: D: Valaciclovir. Alternatives to aciclovir: valaciclovir or famciclovir.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man on chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia has widespread vesicles in several dermatomes and on his trunk and limbs. He is febrile at 38.9°C, with a pulse rate of 112 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Severe or disseminated shingles, especially in the immunocompromised, is treated with IV aciclovir.

steps.x: Disseminated shingles in an immunocompromised patient.

elim: Inadequate for severe disseminated shingles.
Does not treat VZV.
Severe disease in an immunocompromised patient needs IV therapy.
Treats pain, not the infection.

steps.x: B: IV aciclovir. Severe shingles: IV aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with HIV and a CD4 count of 380 cells/µL has a 3 day history of a painful vesicular rash in the left T5 dermatome. She is well, eating and drinking, and the rash involves only one dermatome.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Immunocompromised patients with moderate disease are given oral aciclovir within 7 days of rash onset.

steps.x: Immunocompromised, moderate disease, within 7 days.

elim: She is immunocompromised and within 7 days, so antivirals are indicated.
For severe disease; she has moderate, single-dermatome disease.
Does not treat VZV.
For post-exposure prophylaxis, not active shingles.

steps.x: C: Oral aciclovir. Immunocompromised with moderate disease: oral aciclovir within 7 days.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a 2 day history of shingles over the right T9 dermatome and has started aciclovir. He has mild aching pain over the area. He has no other medical problems or allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his pain?
questions.e: Mild pain in shingles is managed with paracetamol and ibuprofen.

steps.x: Mild pain only.

elim: Reserved for severe neuropathic pain.
Not needed for mild pain.
Reserved for severe neuropathic pain.
Not first-line for mild pain.

steps.x: C: Paracetamol and ibuprofen. Mild pain: paracetamol and ibuprofen; neuropathic agents for severe pain.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has post-herpetic neuralgia in the left T6 dermatome 4 months after shingles. Gabapentin did not help and caused dizziness. She also has low mood and poor sleep.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate alternative?
questions.e: Antidepressants such as amitriptyline or duloxetine are options for post-herpetic neuralgia.

steps.x: Neuropathic pain after gabapentin failed, with poor sleep.

elim: The infection has resolved.
Not a treatment for neuropathic pain.
Ineffective for neuropathic pain.
Does not treat neuropathic pain.

steps.x: B: Amitriptyline. PHN options: gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline, duloxetine.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl has chickenpox. She has a fever of 38.3°C and is itchy but drinking well. Her father asks which medicine to give for the fever.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
questions.e: Chickenpox in children is supportive with calamine and paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs.

clues: which medicine to give for the fever
steps.x: A well child who needs symptom relief.

elim: NSAIDs increase the risk of necrotising fasciitis.
Not routinely needed in a healthy child.
No bacterial infection.
Steroids worsen VZV infection.

steps.x: E: Paracetamol and calamine lotion. Calamine and paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs (necrotising fasciitis risk).

questions.stem: An 8 year old boy developed chickenpox 3 days ago. He is well, but some lesions are still weeping vesicles and new spots appeared this morning. His mother asks when he can go back to school.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Only after a negative PCR test
When all lesions have crusted over
questions.e: Children with chickenpox are excluded from school until all lesions are crusted.

clues: when he can go back to school
steps.x: Lesions still active.

elim: Exclusion is based on crusting, not fever.
Too long.
He is still infectious.
Testing is not needed.

steps.x: E: When all lesions have crusted over. Exclude from school until all lesions are crusted over.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 22 weeks pregnant developed an itchy vesicular rash on her trunk 10 hours ago. Her VZV IgG from early pregnancy was negative. She is well, with normal breathing and oxygen saturation of 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A non-immune pregnant woman with a chickenpox rash gets oral aciclovir within 24 hours of rash onset.

clues: VZV IgG from early pregnancy was negative
steps.x: Non-immune, rash under 24 hours.

elim: A non-immune pregnant woman with a rash needs antivirals.
NSAIDs are avoided in pregnancy and in chickenpox.
Not indicated.
Reassurance is only for immune women.

steps.x: D: Oral aciclovir. Non-immune with rash: oral aciclovir within 24 hours.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 18 weeks pregnant was exposed to her niece's chickenpox 3 days ago. Her VZV IgG result has just come back positive. She has no rash and is well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: An immune pregnant woman needs reassurance only.

clues: VZV IgG result has just come back positive
steps.x: She is immune.

elim: She is immune.
Not needed when immune.
Not indicated.
Only for non-immune women.

steps.x: B: Reassure her. Immune pregnant woman: reassurance only.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man attends for his annual review. He had chickenpox as a child and is well. He asks whether he can do anything to reduce his risk of shingles as he gets older.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
questions.e: The shingles vaccine is offered to everyone at age 65.

steps.x: Age 65 asking about prevention.

elim: Not used for prevention.
Shingles is reactivation of his own latent virus.
Not useful.
The vaccine is offered at 65.

steps.x: D: Offer the shingles vaccine now. Shingles vaccine offered at 65.

questions.stem: A child develops chickenpox 2 weeks after sitting next to a classmate with the infection. Her mother asks what type of organism causes it and how it spread.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate answer?
o: A double-stranded DNA herpesvirus spread by droplets and vesicle fluid
A Gram-positive bacterium spread by skin contact
A single-stranded RNA virus spread by mosquitoes
An enterovirus spread by the faecal-oral route
questions.e: VZV is a double-stranded DNA herpesvirus spread by respiratory droplets and direct contact with vesicle fluid.

steps.x: Close contact spread.

elim: VZV is a virus.
Describes HIV.
Describes dengue.
Describes hand, foot and mouth.

steps.x: A: A double-stranded DNA herpesvirus spread by droplets and vesicle fluid. VZV: dsDNA herpesvirus, droplets and vesicle fluid.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has shingles in the right C6 dermatome, along the thumb side of the forearm. A student asks where the virus was before it reactivated.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of latency?
questions.e: After primary infection VZV is latent in the dorsal root ganglia; it travels down a single sensory nerve.

steps.x: A single dermatome rash.

elim: Motor neurones are not the site of VZV latency.
Not where VZV is latent.
Not a site of latency.
VZV replicates here during rash but is not latent there.

steps.x: C: Dorsal root ganglion. Latency in the dorsal root ganglia.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman develops shingles in the left T10 dermatome. She is otherwise well and takes no immunosuppressants. A student asks why shingles is more common in older people and why only one strip of skin is affected.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate explanation?
o: Antibody loss with spread through the blood
New infection with spread via lymphatics
Reduced skin barrier with spread along veins
Vaccine failure with spread down motor nerves
Waning cell-mediated immunity with spread down one sensory nerve
questions.e: Reactivation occurs as cell-mediated immunity declines with age, and the virus travels down one sensory nerve.

steps.x: Age-related immunity and a dermatomal rash.

elim: Spread is along a nerve, not the blood.
Shingles is reactivation, not new infection.
Not the mechanism.
VZV travels down sensory nerves.

steps.x: E: Waning cell-mediated immunity with spread down one sensory nerve. Falling cell-mediated immunity; virus travels down a single sensory nerve.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has severe burning pain and allodynia in the right T7 dermatome 6 months after shingles has healed. He asks why the pain continues when the rash has gone.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Continued active viral replication in the skin
Ongoing nerve damage and inflammation in the affected dermatome
questions.e: Post-herpetic neuralgia results from ongoing nerve damage and inflammation after the rash resolves.

steps.x: Neuropathic pain long after the rash.

elim: Not related to persistent dermatomal pain.
There are no signs of infection.
The rash has resolved.
Does not cause allodynia in a dermatome.

steps.x: E: Ongoing nerve damage and inflammation in the affected dermatome. PHN = ongoing nerve damage and inflammation.

questions.stem: A neonate born to a non-immune mother who had chickenpox at 10 weeks of gestation has a hypoplastic left leg and dermatomal scarring. A student asks how the infection caused these defects.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Maternal fever causing neural tube failure
Transplacental viral spread disrupting developing limb buds
questions.e: Transplacental transmission in the first trimester disrupts limb buds and causes dermatomal scarring.

steps.x: First-trimester infection and limb defect.

elim: First-trimester defects are not caused at delivery.
Aciclovir is not teratogenic in this way.
Not the mechanism.
Does not explain limb hypoplasia and scarring.

steps.x: E: Transplacental viral spread disrupting developing limb buds. Transplacental VZV in the first trimester disrupts limb buds.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy with chickenpox has been given regular ibuprofen by his parents. On day 5 he has a very painful, rapidly spreading red area on his thigh and is febrile and tachycardic. A student asks why ibuprofen is discouraged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: It increases viral replication in the skin
It may mask early bacterial infection and impair the inflammatory response
questions.e: NSAIDs are thought to mask early signs of secondary bacterial infection and impair the immune response, raising necrotising fasciitis risk.

steps.x: NSAIDs, chickenpox and a spreading infection.

elim: Not a feature of ibuprofen in chickenpox.
Linked to aspirin, not ibuprofen.
Not the mechanism given.
Not the reason it is avoided.

steps.x: D: It may mask early bacterial infection and impair the inflammatory response. NSAIDs in chickenpox mask infection and increase necrotising fasciitis risk.
